TODDLER 2 · LESSON 8

First Concepts for Toddlers: Big, Small, Up & Down

Age 18–24 MonthsSubject Think & TalkClass Toddler 2Duration 3–5 minutes

Around eighteen to twenty-four months, toddlers love spotting differences: the big ball and the little ball, the box that opens and shuts, the cup that is full and then empty. This class uses eleven realistic pictures arranged in concept pairs — big and small, up and down, open and closed, full and empty, one and many, and in — shown one at a time in pair order, so each opposite appears right after its partner and the comparison is easy to see. Then the last game continues off screen: put a toy in a basket, take it out, and do it again.

There is no script and nothing to test. Show a pair, say the concepts clearly — ‘Big. Small.’ — and give your toddler time to look at the difference. Short, playful sessions of three to five minutes are all it takes.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to Teach First Concepts

Show the two cards in a pair one after the other and say the concept clearly. For example: ‘Big. Small.’ Give your toddler time to look at the difference.

Repeat the concepts naturally using real objects and everyday moments. You can show a big ball and a small ball, open and close a box, or point out when a cup is full or empty.

Keep the activity playful. Your toddler does not need to name every concept or answer questions correctly.

Every child develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Big ball. Small ball.
  • Up! Now down.
  • Open the box. Close the box.
  • The cup is full. Now it’s empty.
  • One duck. Many ducks.
  • The ball is in the basket. Now take it out!
REAL-WORLD CONNECTION

Practice Around the House

Keep these activities parent-supervised and simple.

  • Big & Small: Find one big object and one small object.
  • Up & Down: Lift a toy up, then bring it down.
  • Open & Closed: Open and close a safe box or container together.
  • Full & Empty: Show a cup with water and an empty cup during an appropriate supervised activity.
  • One & Many: Show one toy, then a small group of toys.
  • In & Out: Put a toy in a basket, then take it out.

    Big — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the concept pairs with the easiest win: big, said with wide arms and a big voice. Your toddler compares the card with the real things nearby, and the word grows into a gesture.

    What is this?

    Big is a size word — it points at the larger of two things. Alone it floats; next to something small it lands. The card shows one large object filling the frame, so the word has a whole picture to live on.

    What does it mean?

    Size words only make sense as comparisons, and the body teaches them first: arms stretched wide are a toddler’s definition of big long before the word is. Gesture and word grow up together here.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect the arms-out gesture first, a big-bee! second, and the clean word last — every stage counts as the lesson working. At this age, understanding shows up in the pointing, not the pronunciation.

    Why this matters

    Big hides in every room: the big chair, the big door, the big dog next door. A word this findable gets rehearsed all day, and the pair-card (small) makes it sharper whenever you show them together.

    What it teaches

    Size vocabulary, comparison-making, and gesture-word pairing — the first abstract idea a toddler owns, taught entirely with arms.

    Words to learn

    bigsmallwidegiantarmsstretch

    Say this to your child

    “"Biiig! Look at this — arms out wide, big! Can you stretch big like me? Now look: this ball is big… this one is not so big. Where is the big one? Yes! Big arms for the big ball."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and fill yourself with it: stretch your arms out wide and say biiig — the whole body pronouncing the word.
    2. Invite the copy: can you stretch like this? Big arms! Let your toddler’s body answer before their mouth does.
    3. Bring two real objects — one big, one small — and lay them side by side. Touch the big one: big! Touch the small one and shake your head gently: not big.
    4. Let your toddler take the pointing turn: where is the big one? A hand landing on the larger object is the whole concept, arrived.
    5. Hunt one big thing per day this week — the big chair, the big ball, the big door — always with arms out, so gesture and word stay welded.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a large object demonstrating the concept big for toddlers — one big thing, filling the whole picture. Ask your toddler to stretch their arms wide like the big thing takes up all the room.

    Ask your child

    "Can you stretch out big?" "Which one is the big ball?" "Where is something big in this room?" "Is the chair big or is the button big?"

    What your child can say or do

    Arms wide first, always — the gesture is the answer for months. Words arrive as bee, beeg or a proud BIG! with everything they own stretched out. Some toddlers answer by grabbing the bigger of two objects; the grabbing is the comparison made visible.

    Out in the real world

    Big lives everywhere your toddler looks: the big spoon, the big step, the big dog at the fence. One arms-out big per outing keeps the word stretching along with them.

    Try it together

    Big-small race: set two balls, two cups, two books on the rug and call the sizes — big! — and let your toddler slap the winner. You point and name, they pounce; the body learns what the mouth will say.

    Understanding check

    Hold up the big card beside the small card and ask for the big one. An instant reach, an arms-out, or a point at the large card all pass. Then try it with real spoons — transfer from picture to kitchen is the gold star.

    Parent tips

    Put your whole face into the word: biiig. Exaggeration is not silliness here — it is the teaching. Show the pair back to back, big then small, because opposites explain each other faster than either explains alone.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle here beyond the usual floor-games rule: the comparing objects stay bigger than a toilet-roll tube and softer than a bruise. The stretching, at least, is risk-free.

    This lesson pairs with the Big flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    Small — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson brings the pair’s second half: small, taught in a whisper with a curled-up body. Right after big, the contrast does the teaching — your toddler feels the difference in their own arms.

    What is this?

    Small is a size word for the tiny end of things — the crumb, the pea, the button. The card shows one small object, and the whisper-voice gives the word a body of its own.

    What does it mean?

    Small is learned against big, never alone: show the two cards back to back and the comparison does the work. Small things also carry a built-in rule toddlers love — tiny things get tiny voices.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a curled-up curl, a whisper, or a pointed finger at the tiniest thing in sight — all are the word arriving. The hunt matters more than the naming, and tiny treasures get inspected closely.

    Why this matters

    Small things are a toddler’s favourite currency: buttons, pebbles, crumbs of biscuit. A size word attached to beloved tiny objects gets used with passion.

    What it teaches

    Size comparison on the second pole, whisper-voice control, and visual searching for tiny targets — fine attention dressed as treasure hunting.

    Words to learn

    smalllittletinywhispercurlfingers

    Say this to your child

    “"Small! So tiny — whisper it: sssmall. Can you curl up small like a mouse? Look — a big block, and a small block. Where is the small one? Yes… whisper it with me: small."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the big card first — one big arms-out — then the small card, and shrink everything: curl your body small, squeeze your arms in, whisper smaaall.
    2. Invite the copy: can you curl up small? A toddler curling into a ball is the concept taking over their whole body.
    3. Lay out two objects again — the big one, the small one — and let the whisper land on the right one: this one is… smaaall.
    4. Send the hunt: find something small in this room! Follow the pointing finger and whisper the word over every tiny treasure found.
    5. Keep the pair alive all week: big bite, small bite; big step, small step. The contrast is the lesson; repeat it wherever two sizes meet.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a small object demonstrating the concept small for toddlers — one tiny thing, sitting in lots of empty space. Ask your toddler to curl up small next to it, then to point very gently, with one finger.

    Ask your child

    "Can you curl up small?" "Which one is small?" "Can you whisper the word?" "Where is something tiny in this room?"

    What your child can say or do

    A body curl, a whisper that is mostly air, or smaaall delivered like a secret — all are answers. Expect small and big to swap houses for a while; the confusion is the comparison being built, and it settles on its own schedule.

    Out in the real world

    The house is full of small: the button, the pea, the crumb, the sock. Small hunts work at the table, in the garden, on the walk — anywhere tiny things gather.

    Try it together

    Tiny treasure hunt: scatter a few safe, too-big-to-swallow objects and one genuinely small (but choke-safe) item, and hunt the smallest together — whispering all the way. The whisper keeps the game slow and the eyes sharp.

    Understanding check

    Show both cards and ask for the small one. A correct point, a curl, or a whisper all pass. Then hold up two real objects — a small win on kitchen goods means the idea has left the cards and settled in.

    Parent tips

    Whisper the word — the voice-drop is what makes small memorable, and it buys you calm in the middle of any loud day. Keep showing the pair: small means nothing without big standing next to it.

    Staying safe

    Small is the one concept with a built-in hazard: anything genuinely tiny goes straight in the mouth at this age. The hunt uses choke-safe objects only, and every real small thing stays supervised or out of reach.

    This lesson pairs with the Small flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    Up — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the most requested direction in toddler life — up! — and gives it a card, a gesture and a game: arms high, toys flying, and the word rising with the voice.

    What is this?

    Up is a direction word — the way your arms go, the way the bubble goes, the way you lift your toddler. The card shows an object positioned up, and the pointing finger knows exactly where to go.

    What does it mean?

    Up is learned with the body first: the lift, the reach, the stretched fingers. Saying it with a rising voice while arms go up welds the sound to the direction — pitch and position teaching together.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect the raised-arms gesture, a demanding up!, or a pointed finger at the ceiling — all are answers, and the pointing counts first. Lift requests are fair payment for this lesson.

    Why this matters

    Up is in constant demand: up to be carried, up to the shelf, balloons, birds, aeroplanes. A word with this many live applications rehearses itself every hour of the day.

    What it teaches

    Direction vocabulary, gesture-word linking, and reaching-and-lifting coordination — the physical grammar of space, installed with giggles.

    Words to learn

    uphighliftskyreachrise

    Say this to your child

    “"Up! Reach up high — can you touch the sky? Uuuup! Watch the block go up, up, up… and down. Up! Want me to lift you? Say up — and uuuup you go!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and send your arm up: up! — arm rising, voice rising with it, finger pointing at the ceiling.
    2. Invite the reach: can you go up? Both arms over the head is the toddler signature — let them hold the pose.
    3. Fly a toy: lift a soft block slowly from floor to ceiling saying uuuup the whole way, and let your toddler’s eyes ride along.
    4. Answer the real request with the word attached: up? Up! — and lift. The word and the reward land in the same second, which is how it sticks.
    5. Hunt ups all week: birds, bubbles, kites, lamps, the moon. Point, stretch, say the word — the sky is the second deck.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an object positioned up for toddler concept learning — one thing placed high. Ask your toddler to point at it, then stretch their own arms as high as they will go.

    Ask your child

    "Can you reach up high?" "Where did the block go?" "Which way is up?" "What else lives up high?"

    What your child can say or do

    Raised arms are the first answer, an insistent up! the second, and a pointed ceiling the third — every version counts. Expect lift requests to spike during this lesson; that is the word doing exactly what it should.

    Out in the real world

    Ups fill the sky and the house: the lamp, the kite, the aeroplane’s drone, the balloon at the party. One named up per outing keeps the direction pointing the right way.

    Try it together

    Up-and-hold: lift your toddler up on request — up! — and hold for one delighted second before the landing. Three rounds is a workout for both of you and a vocabulary lesson wearing a fairground costume.

    Understanding check

    Ask for up from across the room: can you show me up? Raised arms, a point at the ceiling, or a lifted-object demonstration all pass. Then watch a bubble rise together — if up arrives unprompted, the word owns the sky.

    Parent tips

    Let the voice rise as the arm rises — the pitch teaches as much as the word. Give the real lifts generously and happily; a word that pays in actual flights is a word worth saying.

    Staying safe

    Lifting means lifting safely: bend with your knees, keep the flight short, and stay clear of ceiling fans and lamps. The reaching game stays on the floor — toddlers who learn up will soon try it on chairs.

    This lesson pairs with the Up flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    Down — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lands the pair: after up comes down, taught with a crouch, a drop, and a voice that slides downward. Show the two cards back to back and the contrast does the teaching.

    What is this?

    Down is a direction word — the way the ball goes, the way you crouch, the way everything dropped ends up. The card shows an object positioned down, and the floor is its natural address.

    What does it mean?

    Down is physical comedy for toddlers: things that go down usually land with a satisfying noise. The word rides the drop, and the crouch puts your toddler’s own body into the lesson.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a crouch, a drop performed on cue, or dow! said at the landing — all are answers. The word arrives mid-action best: say down as the ball falls, not after it stops.

    Why this matters

    Down is the most demonstrated direction in the house — cups off tables, blocks off trays, toddlers down slides. A word this well-illustrated by physics needs only naming.

    What it teaches

    Direction vocabulary on the second pole, cause-and-effect delight, and the body knowledge of high and low — spatial grammar with sound effects.

    Words to learn

    downlowdropfloorcrouchfall

    Say this to your child

    “"Down! Crouch down low, low, low… can you touch the floor? Watch the ball — up high… down! It fell down! Say down! Again? Ready… down!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the up card for one beat — up! — then the down card, and slide your voice and your crouch downward: dooown.
    2. Invite the crouch: can you go down low? A toddler folded down to the floor is the word wearing a body.
    3. Drop the ball: hold a soft ball high, say ready… and release on down! The word timed to the fall is the whole lesson in one second.
    4. Let your toddler run the drop: their hand, their timing, your voice on cue. Dropping and naming beats any worksheet ever printed.
    5. Pair them all week: stretch up, fold down; ball up, ball down. The switch is where the concept sharpens — and the giggles are where it stays.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an object positioned down for toddler concept learning — one thing placed low. Ask your toddler to point at it, then to crouch all the way down until their fingers touch the floor.

    Ask your child

    "Can you crouch down low?" "Where did the ball go?" "Which way is down?" "What goes down after up?"

    What your child can say or do

    A crouch, a ball delivered over the edge of the tray with eye contact, or dow! at the thud — all are the lesson landing. Expect repeat requests for the drop; the physics is doing half the teaching.

    Out in the real world

    Down demonstrates itself constantly: the cup pushed off the table, the slide, the stairs, the sun going down. Name the falls gently and the daily crashes become vocabulary.

    Try it together

    Ready-set-drop: stand at the sofa arm with three soft balls, count ready… and drop on down! — then let your toddler call the word while you drop. Caller and dropper swap after three; both jobs teach.

    Understanding check

    Show both cards and ask for down. A crouch, a point at the low card, or a demonstrated drop all pass. Then drop something on purpose in the kitchen — a named down at the thud means the word has left the cards.

    Parent tips

    Say the word as the thing falls — timing is what welds word to event. Keep the pair moving: up-down games beat single-word drills at this age, and the switch is where the thinking happens.

    Staying safe

    The dropping game uses soft balls and safe heights — sofa arms and rug landings only, nothing that bounces toward faces. Crouching toddlers have low centres of gravity but zero judgement: clear the coffee table edges first.

    This lesson pairs with the Down flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    Open — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the second pair with a gesture every toddler can master on the spot: hands unfolding like a flower. Then the real thing — a box, a lid — makes the word do actual work.

    What is this?

    Open is an action word — the state of every door, lid and book that is ready to be used. The card shows an open object, and your hands can show it too, unfolding from fists.

    What does it mean?

    Open is one of the first state words toddlers use correctly, because they request it constantly: open means access, and access means the world. The word pays off the moment it is said.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect unfolding hands, an insistent oh-pen!, or a box offered to you to open — all are answers, and the box-request is the word doing its real job.

    Why this matters

    Open moments are everywhere and always welcome: the biscuit tin, the book, the garden door. A word that unlocks things gets rehearsed with genuine enthusiasm.

    What it teaches

    Action vocabulary, hand-fine-motor work in the unfolding, and state-words — the difference between how things are and how they could be.

    Words to learn

    openwideunfoldliddoorbook

    Say this to your child

    “"Open! Watch my hands — closed tight… and open! Like a flower. Can you do it? Squeeze… open! Now the box: can you open the box? Open! Look what is inside. Open means we can start."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and unfold your closed fists slowly, like a flower opening: ooo-pen. Let the hands do the talking.
    2. Invite the copy: can you open your hands? Squeeze shut, then open wide — the switch is the fun part, and faces can play too.
    3. Bring a real box: can you open it? Help if needed, and say the word at the exact moment the lid comes free — open!
    4. Open a book together and name it there too: open the book — look, the story is open! Every kind of open counts.
    5. Say the word at every real unlock this week: the door, the fridge, the zip. The word should arrive just before the world does.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an open object demonstrating the concept open for toddlers — one thing with its opening showing. Ask your toddler to point at it, then to open their own hands wide like it.

    Ask your child

    "Can you open your hands?" "Can you open the box?" "Where did it open?" "What shall we open next?"

    What your child can say or do

    Unfolding fists, an eager oh-pen! aimed at a locked cupboard, or a box thrust into your arms — all are the word working. Expect open to become a general request for access; that is correct usage, generously interpreted.

    Out in the real world

    Opens run through the whole day: the car door, the lunchbox, the front door after nursery. Say the word each time and the daily unlocking becomes a rolling lesson.

    Try it together

    Flower hands: fists closed like buds, unfolding to blooms on the word open — then close again for closed, which is coming next on the cards. The flower game is the pair’s warm-up act.

    Understanding check

    Hold up the open card and ask what it says. An open! with unfolding hands passes. Then present a closed box — a correct open-request means the word has attached to its real power.

    Parent tips

    Unfold slowly — the slow bloom is what makes the gesture readable. Grant the real opens generously when safe; a word this useful deserves to succeed often, and closed things stay closed when you say so.

    Staying safe

    Open ambitions outrun open permissions: cupboard locks, gate latches and medicine lids exist for good reasons, so the lesson uses the boxes and books you choose. Grown-up hands open what grown-ups keep shut.

    This lesson pairs with the Open flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    Closed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson completes the open pair: closed, taught with fists folding back into buds and a real lid clicking shut. Back to back with open, the two words teach each other.

    What is this?

    Closed is an action word — the state of shut doors, clicked lids and folded hands. The card shows a closed object, and your fists already know how to demonstrate it.

    What does it mean?

    Closed finishes what open starts: neither word is fully clear without the other beside it. The click of a lid is the concept’s sound effect — toddlers remember states best when they change them.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect closing fists, a click-sound made by mouth, or a lid pushed shut with ceremony — all are answers. The switch game (open… closed… open) is where the two words weld together.

    Why this matters

    Closed is the more lawful half of the pair: it ends games, closes books at bedtime, shuts the biscuit tin. Toddlers enjoy the power of both directions equally.

    What it teaches

    State vocabulary in both directions, hand coordination on the fold, and the idea that things have states that change — early physics with sound effects.

    Words to learn

    closedshutlidfistsclicktight

    Say this to your child

    “"Closed! Hands open like a flower… and closed, tight as a bud. Can you do it? Open… closed! Now the box — push the lid… click! Closed. Open, closed, open, closed — you know both!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the open card with blooming hands — then the closed card, and fold the bloom back into a bud: closed. Tight fists, quiet voice.
    2. Invite the copy: open your hands… now close them! The switch is the game; run it three times, slowly.
    3. Bring the real box and close it together: push the lid until it clicks — closed! The click is the word made audible.
    4. Swap fast: open! … closed! … open! — hands, then box, then book. The faster the switch, the harder both brains work, and the louder the laughs.
    5. Name the real closes all week: the book at bedtime, the fridge door, the tap. Closed is the word for endings, and endings deserve their vocabulary too.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a closed object demonstrating the concept closed for toddlers — one thing with its opening shut. Ask your toddler to point at it, then to close their own hands into tight fists just like it.

    Ask your child

    "Can you close your hands?" "Is the box open or closed?" "Can you make the click?" "What did we close today?"

    What your child can say or do

    A fist snap, a click voiced with the mouth, or a lid hammered shut with real purpose — all are the word arriving. Expect door-swinging experiments for a day or two; redirect them to the box and the game survives.

    Out in the real world

    Closes punctuate the day: the biscuit tin sealed, the story finished, the house door shut at night. Name the endings and closed becomes a word with a satisfying sound and a real job.

    Try it together

    Click-the-lid: a small box with a hinged lid, opened and closed on alternating words — your toddler works the lid, you call the states. The click marks every correct change of state like a tiny drum hit.

    Understanding check

    Hold both cards and ask for closed. A fist, a point at the shut card, or a voiced click all pass. Then ask for open… closed… open in a row — three correct switches mean the pair is fully installed.

    Parent tips

    The switch is the lesson: never drill one half of a pair alone. Let your toddler work the lid — the hand does the learning while the mouth files the word, and the click is the reward both directions.

    Staying safe

    Finger pinch is the honest hazard here: hinges, lids and doors bite small fingers, and the click game uses a light-lidded box with grown-up eyes on every close. Doors stay in the slow-motion game only.

    This lesson pairs with the Closed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    Full — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson fills the third pair’s first half: full, taught with a cup, some dry rice, and a brim worth waiting for. Your toddler watches the level rise and the word lands at the top.

    What is this?

    Full is a state word — the container that has everything it can hold. The card shows a full container, and the kitchen supplies the moving version in under a minute.

    What does it mean?

    States change, and the change is where the word lives: the cup goes from not-full to full in front of your toddler’s eyes. Naming the moment of change — there, full! — is what makes the state visible.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect watching, pointing at the brim, or a announced foo! at the top — all are answers. Pouring is the game; the spill is the comedy; the word is the point.

    Why this matters

    Full shows up three times a day: the cup, the bowl, the bath. A state word with mealtimes built in rehearses itself without a single extra minute.

    What it teaches

    State vocabulary, watching a level rise, and cause-and-effect pouring — the fine-motor and cognitive gains share the same cup.

    Words to learn

    fulltopfillcupbrimmore

    Say this to your child

    “"Full! Watch the cup — pouring, pouring, more and more… there! Right to the top. Full! Can you say full? Now you pour… careful… careful… FULL! Right to the brim. Full up!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and trace the idea with your finger: full — right to the top, not one drop more.
    2. Set out a clear cup and a jug of dry rice, and pour slowly while your toddler watches the level climb: more… more… and — full! Stop at the brim on the word.
    3. Let your toddler try the pour, with your hands hovering: fill it up! Say full together when the top arrives.
    4. Too-full is the sequel: add one extra grain past the brim and let the tiny scandal spill. Full has an edge, and the edge is worth meeting once.
    5. Catch the real states all week: the cup at lunch, the bath filling, the basket of blocks. Say the word when the top arrives, not before.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows a full container demonstrating the concept full for toddlers — one container, filled right up. Ask your toddler to point at the top, where the fullness reaches the brim.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the cup full?" "Can you say full?" "Is your cup full yet?" "What happens if we add more?"

    What your child can say or do

    A pointed finger at the brim, a solemn full!, or a pour that stops exactly when you say the word — all are answers. Expect the word attached to requests too: more! is full’s hungry cousin.

    Out in the real world

    Meals run this lesson: the cup fills, the bowl empties, the bath rises. Two named fulls a day and the state word lives where the eating happens.

    Try it together

    Fill-the-basket: pour blocks into a basket together, slowly, until it is full to the top — then tip it all out for the empty card, coming next. The pair shares one basket and one mess.

    Understanding check

    Show the card and ask where the cup is full. A point at the top, a full!, or a demonstrated pour-to-the-brim all pass. Then watch lunch: a toddler who announces full when their own cup tops up has taken the lesson to the table.

    Parent tips

    Say the word at the moment the top arrives — the timing is the teaching. Use dry rice instead of water for less mopping and more replay; the spill is part of the fun, and the floor forgives rice.

    Staying safe

    Rice and water both end up on the floor and, briefly, in mouths: stay close, sweep promptly, and keep the pour small enough to finish. Water play of any kind at this age is arms-reach-only, every second.

    This lesson pairs with the Full flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    Empty — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson tips the pair upside down: after full comes empty, taught with a dramatic pour, an empty cup held upside down, and the refilling that makes both words true in turn.

    What is this?

    Empty is a state word — the container with nothing left inside. The card shows an empty container, and your toddler can make one in three seconds flat, with sound effects.

    What does it mean?

    All-gone tends to be a toddler’s first take on empty, and it arrives with real feeling: empty is where the snack went. The word gives the gone a shape, and the refill proves states come back.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a dramatic tip-out, an announced ahh-gone or ehm-ty, or an upside-down cup displayed at eye level — all are answers. The pour is the lesson; the word is the commentary.

    Why this matters

    Empties happen daily and demand attention: the finished bowl, the box at the bottom, the cup at the end. A word for the aftermath turns every finished thing into a small ceremony.

    What it teaches

    State vocabulary on the second pole, dumping-and-filling play, and the first hint that states reverse — full comes back, empty goes away, and both have words.

    Words to learn

    emptygonetippouroutcup

    Say this to your child

    “"Empty! Tip it out — pshhh — all gone! The cup is empty. Look inside… nothing there! Empty! Now fill it up again… full! And empty! Full, empty, full, empty — you can make it happen either way."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the full card for one beat — full! — then the empty card, and hold the card upside down to show nothing falls out: empty.
    2. Tip the real cup: pour the rice out slowly into the bowl and say the state change out loud — it was full… now it is empty! All gone.
    3. Hold the empty cup upside down together: look — nothing in there! Empty! Let your toddler check inside, just to be sure.
    4. Refill and repeat: full! … empty! … full! The switch is the game, and the pouring is the motor-skill bonus nobody mentions.
    5. Name the day’s real empties: the bowl after breakfast, the block box tipped out, the bath at the end. Empty gets said at every finish line.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an empty container demonstrating the concept empty for toddlers — one container with nothing left inside. Ask your toddler to point at it, then to look inside their own cup and report.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the empty cup?" "Can you tip it out?" "Is it full or empty?" "Where did everything go?"

    What your child can say or do

    A triumphant dump, all-gone delivered with both arms out, or ehm-ty aimed at the upturned cup — all are the word arriving. Some toddlers check the cup twice for missing contents; the double-check is honest science.

    Out in the real world

    Empties mark the day’s finish lines: the empty plate, the empty bath, the empty bag at the shops. Name them warmly and every ending gains a word.

    Try it together

    Fill-and-spill: one basket, one pile of blocks — fill it high (full!) and tip it low (empty!), again and again. The game is the pair in physical form, and the tidying is suspiciously built in.

    Understanding check

    Show both cards and ask for empty. A point, a dump, or an all-gone with open arms all pass. Then watch the next meal finish — an announced empty at the clean bowl means the word works without the cards.

    Parent tips

    Honour all-gone as true speech — it is empty in toddler grammar, and both are welcome. Keep the refill close behind the tip-out; states that return are states that make sense.

    Staying safe

    The dumping is real and so is the debris: rice, blocks and water all become floor hazards the second after the lesson, and a runner on a wet floor is a slipping hazard. Sweep at once; the game keeps better than the floor does.

    This lesson pairs with the Empty flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    One — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the numbers with the only one that matters yet: one. Taught with a single finger, a single block, and single kisses, one becomes the number with a body and a meaning.

    What is this?

    One is the number word for a single thing — no crowd, no confusion. The card shows one object alone, and the finger you hold up is the number’s oldest, clearest picture.

    What does it mean?

    One is the number the rest of counting stands on: a toddler who owns one can feel two as one-and-another, and many as more than one. It is less a sum than a discovery — this much, and no more.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a finger held up — wobbly, or a fist with one knuckle escaping — and eventually a wan! spoken with it. The gesture is the number; the word rides along whenever it is ready.

    Why this matters

    One runs through daily life as the fair-share number: one biscuit, one book, one more kiss. A number attached to real hand-overs teaches itself at every transaction.

    What it teaches

    Number-word one, one-to-one handing, and the finger-symbol for one — the seed of all counting, planted with a single gesture.

    Words to learn

    onesinglefingeralonefirstmore

    Say this to your child

    “"One! Look — one finger. Just one. Here is one block for you… one! Can you show me one finger? There it is! One kiss… one more. One is just one, all by itself."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and hold up one finger beside it: one. Just the one finger — let the number be the whole show.
    2. Hand over one block, slowly, with the word: one block for you. Then wait. Then one more? — and hand a second: now there are two blocks. One makes others possible.
    3. Let your toddler try the finger: can you show me one? Any single finger raised — or attempted — is the number arriving.
    4. Hand out the real ones all week: one cracker, one sock, one kiss. Say one as each lands, one event per word.
    5. Read one in books too: one duck, one moon, one ball. The word travels light and lands everywhere.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows one object demonstrating the concept one for toddlers — a single thing, alone in the picture. Ask your toddler to hold up one finger next to it, one finger only.

    Ask your child

    "Can you show me one finger?" "How many blocks?" "Is that one or lots?" "Can I have one kiss?"

    What your child can say or do

    A raised index finger is the classic answer, complete with wobble. Wan! or duh! (for one) arrives with practice; the gesture leads the word by weeks, exactly as it should.

    Out in the real world

    Ones are handed over all day: one banana, one shoe, one hug at the gate. Attach the word at the moment of hand-over and the number keeps honest company.

    Try it together

    One-at-a-time post: your toddler posts one block into the box, receives it back, posts it again — one! each round. Single-file handing is the game, and one gets said until it is worn in.

    Understanding check

    Ask for one finger from across the room. A single finger — even a thumb, even attempted — passes. Then hand over two blocks and ask which is one: a pause before taking means the number is being counted, not just heard.

    Parent tips

    One event, one word: say one as each single thing lands and stay silent between landings — the gaps are what make one mean single. Do not rush two; one has a whole year of work ahead and plenty of everyday jobs.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle here — this is a sitting, handing, finger game. The only note: the objects being counted one by one stay bigger than a toilet-roll tube, as everything does at this age.

    This lesson pairs with the One flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    Many — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson finishes the number pair with the crowd scene: many. One block stands alone, the rest pile up together, and your toddler’s arms learn to say the difference before their mouth does.

    What is this?

    Many means more than one — lots, a handful, a whole crowd. The card shows multiple objects together, and the contrast with the one card is what makes the idea legible.

    What does it mean?

    Many is a comparison wearing a number’s clothes: the pile only reads as many because one stood alone first. Real counting can wait a year — more-than-one is the whole idea, and it is a big one.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect both arms flung wide, a vigorous muh-nee, or a grab of the whole pile at once — all are answers. Counting together aloud is optional garnish; many as more-than-one is the meal.

    Why this matters

    Many shows up wherever toddlers hoard: the block box, the cracker crumbs, the bath toys. A word for the crowd names a daily joy — and pairs with one so both keep their edges.

    What it teaches

    Quantity contrast, gesture-symbols for amount (finger versus arms-wide), and early comparison language — pre-counting skills built on piles.

    Words to learn

    manylotsmorehandfulcrowdplenty

    Say this to your child

    “"Many! Look at all of them — so many! One finger for one… both arms for many! Here is one block… and here are — many blocks! Drop them — ohh, so many! Many means lots and lots."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the one card — one finger — then the many card, and fling both arms wide: so many! The gesture switch is the lesson’s first beat.
    2. Split them for real: one block here, the rest of the pile there. Point at each side: one… many! Let the contrast do the explaining.
    3. Count a little together, out loud and unhurried: one, two, three… and finish with a sweep of the arm — many! The count is garnish; the sweep is the point.
    4. Drop the pile: lift the many handful high and let it clatter down — the noise says many all by itself, and the giggles seal the word.
    5. Name the day’s crowds: many ducks, many crumbs, many cars at the window. Many is the word for abundance, and toddler life is abundant.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows multiple objects demonstrating the concept many for toddlers — a crowd of things, packed together. Ask your toddler to spread their arms wide like the crowd, then to point at each object in turn.

    Ask your child

    "Where are the many things?" "Can you show me many arms?" "Is this one or many?" "What else is there lots of?"

    What your child can say or do

    Both arms wide is the answer, often with the whole body joining. Muh! or mah-nee arrives with practice; a two-fisted grab of the entire pile is many in its most sincere form.

    Out in the real world

    Crowds gather everywhere toddlers look: pigeons on the path, ducks on the pond, biscuits left unattended. Many gets said at each gathering and the word feeds on abundance.

    Try it together

    One-or-many: hold up blocks one at a time (one!) then suddenly a whole fistful (many!) — your toddler’s arms tell you which is which. Swap roles and let them surprise you; surprise fistfuls are the funniest many there is.

    Understanding check

    Show both cards and ask for many. Arms-wide, a point at the crowd, or a grab-at-the-pile all pass. Then set out one block and a small heap: a correct gesture for each means the contrast is truly installed.

    Parent tips

    Keep the gesture pair sacred — one finger, two arms — because the body carries the number until the words catch up. Do not expect real counting; many means lots rather than one, and that is plenty of idea for now.

    Staying safe

    The pile-drop happens on the rug with soft blocks, away from toes and furniture edges. Fistfuls go in mouths at this age — blocks stay big, sweeps stay quick, and the floor gets cleared while the giggles are still going.

    This lesson pairs with the Many flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

    In — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson closes the deck with the most requested position word: in. Taught with a shoebox slot and a pile of blocks, it is the posting game — the concept your toddler can play for twenty minutes without help.

    What is this?

    In is a position word — the state of being inside something. The card shows an object inside a container, and the shoebox with a slot in the lid is that card, made playable.

    What does it mean?

    In earns its keep early: toddlers master it while posting things through slots with ferocious concentration. The mouth collects its word, the fingers collect their workout, and both gains arrive in the same game.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a drop, a posted block, or in! said at the exact moment of disappearance — all are answers. The return trip matters just as much: everything that goes in must come out again.

    Why this matters

    In is happening all day at toddler height: the spoon in the bowl, the teddy in the cot, the whole self in the bath. A word this busy needs only to be attached to the game they already play.

    What it teaches

    Position vocabulary, posting precision (the classic toddler obsession), and in-out reversibility — spatial language and fine motor control sharing one shoebox.

    Words to learn

    ininsideboxpostdropout

    Say this to your child

    “"In! Put the block in the box… in! It went in — did you hear it? Shake the box… they are all in there! Now tip it out — out! — and do it again. In, out, in, out — the best game in the house."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and demonstrate with your own hands: one fist closes over the other — the block is in my hand! In.
    2. Cut a slot in a shoebox lid (grown-up scissors) and hand your toddler a block: can you put it in? Guide the drop and say in! at the moment it disappears.
    3. Let the posting run: block after block, one word each time — in! in! in! The repetition is the point, and the concentration is a bonus nobody has to ask for.
    4. Shake the box and listen together: where did they go? In the box! The word survives even when the blocks are out of sight.
    5. Finish the arc: tip the box and let everything come out — out! — then post it all back in. In and out, the whole cycle, named at both ends.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an object inside a container demonstrating the concept in for toddlers — one thing sitting inside something else. Ask your toddler to point at what went in, then at what holds it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the block?" "Can you put it in?" "Is it in or out?" "What else can we put in the box?"

    What your child can say or do

    A posted block with a pointed look, in! said as ihh! at the disappearance, or the whole fist plunged into the box to check — all are the word arriving. Expect the game to continue long after the lesson ends; that is the plan working.

    Out in the real world

    Ins run through every day: the spoon in the bowl, the teddy in the cot, the toddler in the car seat. Name the landings and the daily insertions all join the same vocabulary.

    Try it together

    The posting game, at full scale: a shoebox with a slot, a pile of large caps and blocks — post, retrieve, repeat. Twenty minutes of quiet concentration is normal; interrupt only for snacks and applause.

    Understanding check

    Ask from across the room: put the block in the box! A correct post — or a correct point at the in card — passes. Then ask where the blocks are: in the box! said or gestured means the word describes reality now.

    Parent tips

    Say in at the moment of disappearance, not before or after — timing is the whole weld. Keep the posted items large and the slot smooth; the game runs on repetition, and repetition needs safe pieces.

    Staying safe

    Posting pieces obey the toilet-roll rule — too big to swallow, since everything posted eventually gets mouth-checked. Grown-up scissors cut the slot, the edges get taped smooth, and the tipping-out happens away from toes.

    This lesson pairs with the In flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).
